title: UK-India Week opens at Warwick, betting on a Gujarat–West Midlands corridor
excerpt: The 10th edition of India Global Forum's flagship event launched in Coventry with a region-to-region pitch linking Gujarat's industry to England's manufacturing heartland.
body:
India Global Forum's UK-India Week 2026 opened on June 23 at the University of Warwick, launching the 10th edition of what organisers call the biggest fixture in the UK-Indian calendar. The opening day, staged as the IGF Smarter Regions Forum, set out to turn warm diplomatic language about the UK-India relationship into concrete deals — and it did so by zeroing in on an unusual pairing: the Indian state of Gujarat and England's West Midlands.

The choice of venue is itself a statement. Rather than convening in London, the milestone edition planted itself in Coventry, in the industrial heartland that gave Britain its car industry, to argue that the next phase of the UK-India partnership will be built region-to-region rather than only capital-to-capital.

## Context & Background

UK-India Week has grown over a decade from a networking event into a fixture that draws ministers, chief executives and investors from both countries. This year it arrives with unusual momentum behind it: the two governments have been moving to deepen economic ties, and business on both sides is hungry for a framework that translates headline announcements into factories, jobs and research partnerships.

The Smarter Regions Exchange that anchored the opening day is designed precisely for that. Its premise is that the most durable growth comes from matching specific regional strengths — a manufacturing cluster here, a research university there — rather than waiting for national-level deals to trickle down.



> **"The Smarter Regions Exchange that anchored the opening day is designed precisely for that."**


## Current Developments

The forum brought together senior figures from government, business, academia and industry to deepen the emerging partnership between Gujarat and the West Midlands. A high-level Government of Gujarat delegation took part, including Mamta Verma, Additional Chief Secretary in the state's Industries and Mines Department, and Dr. Vikrant Pandey, IAS, Additional Principal Secretary to the Chief Minister.

Opening discussions examined how the two regions could build a stronger growth corridor through cooperation in industry, investment, innovation and skills. The day's programme spanned advanced manufacturing, clean energy, life sciences and skills development — sectors where Gujarat's industrial base and the West Midlands' engineering and research strengths overlap most naturally.

The Government of Gujarat also presented its growth story to a UK audience, followed by a fast-pitch showcase featuring representatives from manufacturing, textiles, finance and technology. The aim, organisers said, was to surface concrete partnership opportunities rather than broad memoranda — a deliberate attempt to leave Warwick with deals in motion.

## Diaspora Impact

For the Indian diaspora in Britain, the regional framing matters more than it might first appear. The West Midlands is home to one of the UK's largest and longest-established Indian communities, with deep roots in Coventry, Birmingham, Leicester and the surrounding towns. Many diaspora-owned businesses in manufacturing, engineering and professional services sit exactly in the corridor the forum is trying to formalise.

A Gujarat–West Midlands axis also speaks directly to family and commercial ties that already exist. Gujarati entrepreneurs have long been a backbone of British Asian business life, and a structured corridor could give those informal links a formal channel — easier investment routes, clearer skills pathways for students and workers, and a recognised platform for diaspora firms to scale across both markets.

For NRIs watching from the United States and Canada, the model is worth noting too. If region-to-region partnerships prove more nimble than national agreements, similar templates could emerge linking Indian states with diaspora-heavy regions elsewhere.

## What's Next

UK-India Week runs across multiple days, with the Warwick opening feeding into the broader programme of the 10th edition. The real test will come after the speeches: whether the fast-pitch sessions and the Gujarat delegation's visit convert into announced investments, university tie-ups and skills agreements in the weeks ahead.

For now, the message from Coventry is clear. The UK-India relationship is being rewired to run through regions and their diaspora communities — and the West Midlands, with its Indian-origin population and manufacturing pedigree, intends to be first in line.
